Thandiwe's throat tightened and then opened. She walked out to the microphone and before the band started she said, "This is for my teacher," and pointed. The first song was supposed to be the single. Instead she turned to her pianist and whispered the name of an old hymn Mrs. Dlamini had taught them. He nodded. Thandiwe sang it unaccompanied for the first verse, eyes closed, the whole hall silent, feeling every year of her life rise up through her chest.

Ten minutes before we went on, a kid found me by the loading dock. Maybe nineteen. He said he needed to tell me something, and his voice was shaking. He said that two years ago he was in a really dark place and he listened to our second album every night, the whole thing, and it got him through. He was in college now. He studied music. He rolled up his sleeve and showed me a tattoo of one of our lyrics. I didn't know what to say. I hugged him. Then I walked back into the green room and grabbed the setlist off the wall and a pen. We had a new song we'd never dared to play live, the slow one. I wrote it in at number three. My bandmates looked at me and I just said, "Trust me." My hands were drumming on my thighs the whole walk to the stage. When we hit the first chord of that song I looked out at the crowd and found him, near the front, and played every beat for him.

Grigori sat backstage tuning his cello, listening to the hall fill with the murmur of eight hundred people. His heart was going fast, but not with dread. He had been thinking all day about something he read in Pablo Casals's memoir: that every morning of his life, at ninety, Casals played Bach first, and every morning it was new to him. Grigori had played this suite a thousand times. Tonight he wanted to hear it as if it were the first. He closed his eyes and imagined the opening prelude before anyone had ever played it, just notes on paper waiting. He felt his fingers tingle on the strings. When the stage manager touched his shoulder, he stood and walked out into the light without hurrying. He sat. He set the bow on the string and waited until the hall was absolutely still. Then he played the first phrase and it sounded, even to him, like something he was discovering in the moment, rising and turning and opening outward. He almost laughed.

Open mic night at a little bar in Austin, and I was fourth on the list, and I was going to play a song I wrote myself for the very first time. While I waited I watched the third act, an old guy in a cowboy hat with a voice like gravel who sang a song about his late wife's garden. Simple chords. Plain words. Not a single clever line. The whole room got quiet and two people at the bar were wiping their eyes. My song is full of clever lines. I suddenly could hear how clever it was, how much it was hiding behind. When he finished and they called my name I took my guitar up and, standing there at the mic, I changed the second verse. I said the true thing instead, about my dad leaving, the porch light we kept on. My voice cracked on it. I kept going. When I got off the stage the cowboy caught my arm and nodded, and I went straight to a corner table with a napkin to write the rest of it.

Ana-Maria peered through the gap in the curtain as the concert hall filled, and found herself watching a little girl in the front row clutching a tiny violin case on her lap, the smallest size, maybe a sixteenth. The girl couldn't have been older than five. She was staring at the empty stage with an expression of complete, fierce attention. Ana-Maria remembered being that girl in a cold hall in Cluj, watching a soloist and deciding that was what she would be. Her pulse quickened. The Mendelssohn concerto had a cadenza she always played exactly as written. Tonight, standing in the wings, she started hearing a variation of it in her head, something brighter, a little reckless, a flourish up high that would make a five-year-old gasp. Her fingers pressed silently against her palm, testing it. When the conductor raised his baton she was still hearing it. When the cadenza came she played it, the new version, the girl's version, and out of the corner of her eye she saw the small face light up.

The box was heavy and the return address was a town in Vermont I didn't recognize. Inside, wrapped in newspaper, were six battered field notebooks and a letter. They belonged to Dr. Whitcombe, my ornithology advisor, the one I disappointed when I left the doctoral program twelve years ago. She was retiring, she wrote, and clearing her office, and she wanted these to go to the student who used to see what everyone else missed. I opened the first notebook. Pencil sketches of warblers, wind direction, tiny notes in the margins: heard but not seen, check again at dawn. My chest felt tight and bright at the same time. I hadn't held binoculars in years. I went to the hall closet and found them in their case, the strap cracked. That evening I walked to the marsh at the edge of town and stood in the reeds until the light was nearly gone, and when a marsh wren started singing I wrote it down in a fresh notebook, with the time and the wind, just like she did.

Nikolai had no idea who would send him a package, and he turned the small padded envelope over twice in the hallway before opening it. Inside were forty tiny paper packets of seeds, each labeled in careful handwriting: Cherokee Purple tomato, Georgian bean from grandmother Nino, Armenian cucumber, saved 2019. A note explained that the sender ran a seed library in Tbilisi and had found Nikolai's name on an online forum, where he'd once posted about his father's lost tomato variety. One of the packets said simply: Mtsvane, your father's kind, I think. Nikolai sat down on the stairs. He held that packet up to the light and could see the seeds inside, flat and pale. He had a tiny balcony and no garden. That did not matter. By the afternoon he had written to the community garden, phoned his cousin about the empty lot behind her house, and bought a bag of potting soil on the way home, carrying it up four flights on his shoulder, already counting out which seeds would go first.

The delivery guy needed help carrying the box up the stairs, and when I finally cut it open there was a sewing machine inside. An old one, black and gold, heavy as an anvil. My aunt Fernanda's. There was a note in her loopy writing: I'm too old to see the needle and you're the only one in this family who ever asked how it worked. I sat on the floor of my apartment and ran my fingers over the gold decals. I remembered sitting under her table as a kid, watching her feet on the treadle, fabric pouring off the edge like water. I had spent the last two years saying I wanted to make my own clothes. I'd saved a hundred photos. I'd bought fabric I never touched. Now I pulled it all out of the closet and spread it on the floor: a green linen, a printed cotton with lemons on it. I found a pattern for a simple skirt online. By midnight I had the machine threaded, my tongue between my teeth, and I was sewing my first seam.

Precious hadn't ordered anything, so the package on her doorstep puzzled her. Inside was a hardcover book, a novel, by an author whose name took her a moment to place. Then she remembered: Abel Mwangi, the quiet boy in the back row of her English class twenty years ago, who wrote stories in the margins of his math homework. She opened the book and found the dedication. For Mrs. Precious Ndlovu, who told me my stories were worth finishing. She read it standing on her porch, and then she sat down on the step because her legs had gone strange. She had retired three years ago, tired and unsure whether any of it had mattered. She read the first chapter right there in the afternoon sun. Then she went inside, found her old lesson notebooks in the closet, and started thinking about the after-school writing club at the library that had closed for lack of volunteers. She picked up the phone. By evening she had a meeting with the librarian set for Thursday.

I don't get mail except bills, so the package with all the foreign stamps caught my eye. It was from a school in Nairobi. Inside were twenty-three letters and drawings from fourth graders. A note from their teacher explained: years ago I donated a box of my old science books to a charity, and somehow they ended up in her classroom, with my name written inside the covers. The children wanted to say thank you. One boy drew me as an astronaut. A girl named Wanjiru wrote that she wants to be a geologist like the man in the book. I am a retired geology teacher. I'm seventy. I laid all the drawings across the dining table and couldn't stop going back to them. Then I went down to the basement where I keep my rock collection, forty years of specimens, labeled. I started picking out the best ones, quartz, obsidian, a trilobite. I'd ship them a whole kit. I started writing the first letter back, to Wanjiru, describing how to tell a mineral by its streak.

Lars recognized the handwriting on the box immediately: his father's oldest friend, Einar, from the boatyard. Inside, rolled in an oily canvas cloth, were his father's carving chisels. Twelve of them, their wooden handles dark and polished smooth from fifty years in the same hands. A note from Einar said only: He would want you to use them. Lars unrolled the canvas on the kitchen table and lifted them one by one, feeling the weight, the slight dip worn into each handle where his father's thumb had rested. He hadn't carved since he was a teenager, sitting in the corner of the boatyard shop making bad little birds out of pine scraps. He went out to the woodpile in his parka and found a piece of birch, clean and pale. He sat at the table with a lamp pulled close and started. The first cuts were clumsy. Then his hands began to remember. Hours later his wife came down and found him surrounded by shavings, the rough shape of a seabird emerging under his fingers.

Esperanza and her brother Julio had been clearing their grandmother's sewing room all afternoon in tired silence when Julio opened the cedar chest. Inside were quilts, a dozen of them, and under the quilts a spiral notebook full of patterns drawn in colored pencil. Each one had a name: The Year We Came North. Julio's Baptism. The Flood. And at the very bottom of the chest, an unfinished quilt, half-pieced, with the pattern sketched on the last page: For My Great-Grandchildren. Neither of them could talk for a minute. Then Esperanza spread the unfinished quilt across the bed and started tracing the pattern with her finger, figuring out where each piece went. "I can't sew," Julio said. "I'll teach you," she said, though she barely could herself. She found their grandmother's thimble in a tin and slid it onto her finger. It fit. By nightfall they had cleared the dining table, laid out the fabric squares in order, and Julio was cutting the first piece, slowly, while Esperanza read the pattern aloud.

My sister found the diaries in a hatbox at the back of Nana's closet. Five of them, leather, dated 1951 through 1955, and we sat on the bedroom floor and started reading. Nana went to medical school. We had no idea. She was one of three women in her class in Bombay. She wrote about professors who refused to call on her, about studying anatomy by kerosene lamp, about delivering a baby alone at three in the morning at nineteen. Then she married and moved to London and never practiced again, and never told us. I read until my legs went numb. I'm thirty-two. I've been working as a lab tech for eight years, telling myself it's too late for medical school. I kept turning back to one line, underlined twice: Nobody is going to hand you a seat. I took a picture of it with my phone. That night I downloaded the application requirements for the post-baccalaureate program and printed them, and I tucked one of her diaries into my bag so I could read it on the train.

The twins, Rohan and Riya, found the recipe box under their grandmother's sink, wrapped in a plastic bag against the damp. It was overflowing: hundreds of index cards, spattered with turmeric and ghee, in three languages depending on the decade. Some recipes were just lists of ingredients with no amounts, or notes like add until it smells right. Rohan picked up a card for her lemon pickle and started laughing, because he could smell it, actually smell it in his memory. Riya was already sorting the cards into piles on the kitchen floor: sweets, dals, festival dishes. "We should make every single one," she said. "And write them down properly. With amounts." Rohan was already nodding. They could test them on weekends, call the aunties for the missing steps, take photographs. He pulled out his phone and started a shared folder. Riya found a notebook and wrote a title page in big block letters. By the time they finally ate dinner, takeout on the floor among the piles, they had planned the first six weekends.

We knew Grandma Hilde liked to swim. We didn't know until we cleared out her dresser that she had swum the English Channel in 1963. My brother found the certificate rolled in a cardboard tube, and under it a scrapbook: newspaper clippings in German and English, a grainy photo of a young woman slathered in grease, waving from the water at Dover. Fourteen hours and nine minutes. We sat on her bed and read every clipping, passing the scrapbook back and forth. I swim laps three mornings a week. I always stop at a mile because that seems like enough. I looked at that photo of her, arm raised, grinning, salt-streaked, and I felt something rise up through my ribs. "I'm going to swim the lake," I said. "The whole length. Next summer." My brother didn't laugh. He said he'd follow me in a boat. On the drive home I looked up open-water swimming clubs, and the next morning I didn't stop at a mile. I swam two.

Anjali and her two brothers were sorting their grandmother's things into boxes labeled keep and donate when Vikram pulled a long cloth case from under the bed. Inside was a sitar, its gourd painted with faded flowers, the strings slack. None of them had ever heard Nani play. Their mother, on speaker phone, told them Nani had studied seriously as a girl in Lucknow and stopped when she married. Anjali took the sitar onto her lap the way she'd seen musicians do it in videos. It was heavier than she expected. She plucked one string and the sound rang through the empty room, deep and buzzing, and all three of them went silent. Anjali plucked it again. She felt the vibration in her shins and her chest. "I'm taking this," she said, and nobody argued. She took it home that night, wrapped in a blanket on the backseat. She found a teacher in the city who gave lessons on Sundays and emailed him before bed, then sat on the floor tuning the first string by ear, very slowly.

Grandma kept everything, so we expected boxes of junk. What my sister and I found in the filing cabinet in her study were letters. Carbon copies of letters she had written to the city council over forty-one years. Asking for a crosswalk near the school. Asking for streetlights on Delmar. Asking, over and over, for nine years, for the empty lot on Pine to become a park. And there, clipped to the last letter, was the council's response approving it, and a photo of her at the ribbon cutting in a big hat, age seventy-eight. I play in that park. I mean I played in it as a kid, my whole childhood, and I never knew. I sat down in her desk chair and read every letter. Some were fierce, some were funny, all of them were stubborn. I've complained about our city for years and never written one word to anyone. That night I looked up how to run for the neighborhood council seat. The filing deadline was in three weeks. I printed the form and signed it with her pen.

Clementine unlocked the bookshop at eight on Monday and found, among the weekend's mail in the drop slot, a folded piece of notebook paper. It was from a child. Dear Bookstore, it said in pencil, I read the dragon book you have in the window from outside every day on my way to school, I am on page 40, please do not sell it before I finish. Clementine laughed out loud alone in the dark shop, then didn't laugh. She stood by the window display and found the dragon book, open to page forty. Someone had been reading it through the glass. She switched on the lights and walked the aisles, thinking. Kids who couldn't buy books. Kids who read through windows. By nine she had cleared the reading nook in the back, dragged in beanbags from the storeroom, and was writing a sign in her best lettering: Free After-School Reading Hour, Every Day, Ages 6 to 12. She taped it to the window right beside the dragon book, and left the book open at forty-one.

Monday, five a.m., and I unlocked the bakery with sore legs from a weekend of walking around Copenhagen. I'd gone for my cousin's wedding, but what I really remember is a tiny bakery in Nørrebro where the cardamom buns were twisted into knots and so fragrant I ate three standing at the counter. I've been making the same twelve pastries in this shop for nine years. I turned on the ovens and, instead of starting the croissant dough, I pulled out the cardamom pods and the mortar. I crushed them fresh, and the smell filled the whole kitchen. I tried the dough three different ways. The first was too dense. The second was close. The third, I twisted the way I'd watched the baker in Copenhagen do it, a long rope folded and wound, and they came out of the oven golden and craggy and perfect. My assistant arrived at six and stopped in the doorway, sniffing. I handed her one. She ate it in silence and then said, "Put these in the window." I was already writing the new chalkboard.

Desmond had run the hardware store on Harmon Street for thirty-eight years, and on Monday mornings he always unlocked the door, flipped the sign, and made coffee. But this Monday he stopped on the sidewalk with his keys in his hand. Over the weekend someone had painted a mural on the brick wall of the laundromat across the street: a huge swirl of birds and flowers and faces, kids from the neighborhood, all in colors so bright they hurt. A young woman was up on a ladder adding the last touches. Desmond turned around and looked at his own store. The sign was peeling. The window display hadn't changed since 2011. He felt something kick in his chest. He crossed the street and asked the young woman what she charged for signs. She grinned and climbed down. By noon they had sketched a new sign together on the back of a paint sample card, and Desmond had cleared the dusty window and was arranging bright watering cans and seed packets in it, whistling like a man forty years younger.

I opened the flower shop on Monday at seven, as always, my van loaded from the wholesale market. Most Mondays are slow, wedding orders from the weekend done, nothing ahead. But this morning at the market I'd seen something I couldn't stop thinking about: an old Dutch grower arranging his own unsold flowers into a bucket in the back of his truck, purely for himself, wild and lopsided, tulips with branches and dried grasses and one huge artichoke flower. It was the most beautiful thing in the whole warehouse. I'd been making the same tidy round bouquets for years because they sell. I hauled every bucket in and then, instead of making the usual stock, I cleared the whole front window. I built an arrangement as tall as me, crooked and alive, quince branches, ranunculus, wheat, a single giant protea. I kept stepping back out onto the sidewalk to look at it, then running back inside to change something. A woman stopped on her way to the train and stared. Then she came in and asked, "Can you make me something like that?"

Lucas unlocked the bike shop at eight on Monday and noticed, as he hadn't on any Monday before, how many commuters were rolling past on the new bike lane. Dozens. A woman with a toddler seat. A man in a suit on a folding bike. Two teenagers in school uniforms. Half of them, he could tell even from the door, had underinflated tires or squeaking chains. He stood there with his coffee getting cold, counting. Then an idea arrived so fully formed that he laughed. A free fifteen-minute tune-up station, out front, every Monday morning, rush hour. Pump, lube, brake check, a friendly word. He went into the back and dragged out the old work stand, wheeled it onto the sidewalk, and hung up the floor pump. He wrote a sign on cardboard: FREE MONDAY CHECKUP, NO CATCH. The first person stopped within four minutes, a nurse heading to the hospital, and while Lucas adjusted her brakes he was already planning a Saturday class to teach people to do it themselves.

Every Monday I open the corner store at six, and the first hour is always the same: newspapers, coffee, the bus drivers buying gum. But this Monday Mrs. Achterberg was waiting outside before I even had the shutter up, and she grabbed both my hands. She'd found a job. She found it on the corkboard by my door, where I let people pin notices, a card for a bookkeeping position at the dental office down the road. She'd been unemployed for a year. She started today. She kissed my cheek and ran to catch her bus. I stood there looking at that messy corkboard, the lost cats and guitar lessons and rooms for rent, and I realized it was the most important thing in my shop. I spent the whole morning between customers rearranging it. I cleared the wall beside it too. I made sections: jobs, help needed, help offered. I bought a bigger board at lunch. By closing time I had a sign printed: Community Board, Bring Your Notices, and three people had already pinned new ones.

On my first shift at the food bank, the woman running the sorting line was ninety-one. Her name is Bernadette and she's been doing this since 1983. She wore a cardigan and an apron and moved down the line faster than any of us, checking dates on cans, catching every dented one, calling each volunteer by name after hearing it once. When a family came in, she knew the kids' names, their allergies, which one had just lost a tooth. I watched her lift a crate of potatoes I would have struggled with. On break I asked how she kept going. She shrugged and said, "Somebody's always hungry on Tuesday." That sentence stuck in me like a splinter. I've been drifting for two years since I retired, waiting for my life to become something. I signed up for every Tuesday through December before I left. On the drive home I kept thinking about the empty church kitchen near my house, and how many people in my building eat alone. I pulled over and called the pastor right then.

Kyung-soo had volunteered at the food bank every Saturday for three years, and he knew the regulars. So he noticed when a man he remembered from a hard winter walked in, not with an empty bag but with a pickup truck full of groceries. The man had a job now, he explained, managing a restaurant. Every week the restaurant had extra, and he wanted it to come here. He shook Kyung-soo's hand for a long time. He said, "You guys never once made me feel small." Kyung-soo spent the rest of the shift unloading that truck, and every box he lifted he thought about the man's hand. He kept thinking: how many other restaurants in this town throw food away every night? He started a list on his phone during his break: the pizza place, the sushi bar, the big hotel. By the end of his shift he'd drafted a letter. By the end of the week he had three restaurants signed on and was sketching a pickup route on a map taped to his refrigerator.

I'm sixteen and I started volunteering at the food bank for school credit, honestly. But on my second Saturday I was bagging produce and noticed there was barely any. Mostly canned stuff, boxed pasta, peanut butter. A grandmother asked me if there were any fresh greens and I had to tell her no. She said that was okay, in the voice people use when it isn't okay. I couldn't stop thinking about it. There's a huge empty lawn behind our school that nobody uses. I went home and spent all night reading about school gardens, about how many pounds of kale one raised bed can grow, about grants for youth projects. I made a slideshow. I'm not usually a slideshow person. On Monday I showed it to my biology teacher before first period, talking so fast she had to tell me to breathe. She said she'd help me pitch it to the principal. I've already picked the spot for the first bed, the sunny corner by the gym, and I keep drawing it in the margins of my notebooks.

Marisol was sorting donations when she saw it: a whole pallet of the same random things. Forty cans of chickpeas, sixty boxes of rice, a mountain of carrots that would go soft by Thursday. She'd been a line cook for fifteen years. She knew what that pile could become. She found the coordinator and asked about the kitchen in the back of the church hall. Was it ever used? Not really, he said. Marisol went and stood in it. A six-burner stove, two ovens, pots on hooks. She ran her fingers along the steel counter. In her head she was already roasting the carrots with cumin, simmering chickpeas into a stew, making rice with fried onions on top. Hot meals, not just groceries. And then a step further: teaching people to cook with what they got in their bags. She asked if she could try it on Thursday. The coordinator said yes, mostly to see what would happen. She drove home and wrote a menu on a legal pad, her pen racing, crossing out and adding, until she had five recipes.

I speak Spanish and Haitian Creole, so they asked me to help at the intake table. A woman came in with three small kids and she was trying to explain something to the English-only volunteer, and getting frustrated, and the kids were getting restless. I sat down next to her and asked in Creole what she needed. Her whole face changed. She'd just come from Port-au-Prince, she said, and she didn't know where to find a doctor for her youngest, or how school enrollment worked, or anything. I spent forty minutes with her. I wrote things down, called the clinic, found the enrollment office's number. When she left she held my face in her hands. I sat there afterward feeling like someone had turned up the lights inside me. I'm a sophomore in college. I've been majoring in business because it sounded sensible. That night I opened the course catalog and read every single page about the social work program. I made an appointment with an advisor first thing the next morning.

Augustin had managed logistics for a shipping company for thirty years before he retired, and on his first day volunteering at the food bank he could barely stand still. The line snaked out the door into the cold. Volunteers were walking the length of the warehouse for every item. The canned goods were stacked by donation date, not by type. He bit his tongue for two hours. Then, during the lunch break, he found a stack of paper and started drawing. A U-shaped line. Stations by food group. Pre-packed bags for the most common family sizes. A numbered ticket system so people could sit down instead of standing outside. He was drawing so hard he tore through the paper. When the coordinator came by, he showed her, a little sheepishly. She studied it for a long time and then said, "Can you come in Thursday and help us set it up?" Augustin walked to his car feeling twenty years younger. At home he redrew the whole thing on graph paper and timed each step with a stopwatch in his kitchen.

Femi had been in the surgical waiting room for three hours while they worked on his wife's knee, and a little boy two seats over had been crying for most of it. Then a nurse came out, a tall man with a shaved head and cartoon scrubs, and crouched down to the boy's level. He didn't shush him. He took a glove from his pocket, blew it up into a balloon, drew a face on it with a marker, and gave it the boy's name. The boy stopped crying mid-sob and laughed. The nurse explained to him, simply and honestly, what was happening to his mother. Femi watched the whole thing with his coffee going cold. He had quit nursing school at twenty-four with one semester left. He had always told himself he wasn't the type. Now he could not stop thinking about the way the boy's shoulders had dropped. He opened his phone and searched for the school's re-enrollment policy. He read it twice. He was still drafting the email when the surgeon came out to tell him everything went well.

The waiting room on the pediatric floor has one long wall, and someone covered it with a mural painted by kids who had been patients here. Fish, rockets, a giant purple cat. Every figure had a little name painted beside it and a date. I spent four hours waiting for news about my nephew, and I spent most of them looking at that wall. A girl named Pilar painted a dragon in 2016. A boy named Theo painted a submarine. I kept wondering where they all are now. I teach art at a high school. My students paint the same still lifes every year. And here was this wall, alive, full of kids saying I was here. I asked the receptionist who organized it. She said a volunteer, years ago, who moved away. Nobody had added to it since. By the time the doctor came out to say my nephew was fine, I had filled six pages of my notebook with sketches and plans, and I'd already asked the receptionist for the volunteer coordinator's email.

Beatriz had read every magazine in the oncology waiting room twice, so she picked up a pamphlet from the rack while her father was in for his scan. It was a story about a woman named Lorna, diagnosed with the same cancer as her father. Lorna had started a walking group with other patients, just once a week around the hospital grounds, and it had grown to two hundred people. There was a photo: a crowd in matching green shirts, some in wheelchairs, some bald, all of them laughing in the rain. Beatriz read it three times. Her father had stopped leaving the house. He said he was too tired, too embarrassed. She looked out the window at the courtyard, at the path circling the fountain, and she could see it. She took out her phone and started drafting a flyer. When her father came out of the scan, pale and quiet, she held up the pamphlet and said, "Papá, look at this." He read it slowly. Then he asked, "Green shirts?" and she grinned.

My son needed stitches after falling off his skateboard, and we ended up waiting four hours in the emergency room. Around hour two, a man in a red nose and an enormous bow tie came through the doors with a ukulele. A hospital clown. He went to every kid in that room. He made a crying toddler laugh by pretending his hat was trying to escape. He did a fake magic trick for my son that went spectacularly wrong on purpose. I watched him with my mouth open. I was a stage actor for twenty years before I started selling insurance. I'd forgotten that look on an audience's face, the moment they let go. Watching him, I could feel my old timing come back into my body, my feet wanting to move. When he took a break I followed him into the hallway and asked how he'd gotten into it. He gave me the name of the training program. I wrote it on my son's discharge paperwork. In the car my son asked why I was doing funny voices all the way home.

Ngozi was waiting for her mother to come out of a procedure when a young doctor sat down across from a family nearby and started explaining a diagnosis. He didn't use the clipboard. He took a napkin and drew: a heart, simple, like a child's drawing, with arrows and little smiling valves. The family's little girl leaned in. Ngozi, who illustrated children's books for a living, watched the drawing grow, and something in her clicked into place. She had always wanted to make a book that mattered more than talking ducks. She thought of every worried child sitting in rooms like this one. She pulled out her sketchbook and started drawing: a hospital as a castle, a kind doctor with a stethoscope like a magic necklace, a girl named Ada who asked all the questions. She drew page after page, barely looking up, her pencil racing. When the nurse called her name she startled, stood, and realized she had filled nearly the whole sketchbook, a full story waiting in her hands.

I was waiting for my own scan, just a routine one, when the young man next to me apologized for taking up two chairs with his books. Medical school, second year, studying for his board exams between visits to his grandfather upstairs. He was trying to memorize the cranial nerves and kept mixing up seven and eight. I taught high school biology for thirty-five years. I couldn't help myself. I showed him the old rhyme I used to teach, and then a way to trace them on your own face with your finger. His eyes lit up. He tried it, laughed, got it right. We worked through the whole list before they called my name. Walking back to the imaging room in that ridiculous gown, I felt more alive than I had in the four years since I retired. There must be hundreds of students like him at that university, struggling alone. When I got home I called the medical school's tutoring center and asked if they ever took old teachers, and I spent the evening digging out my anatomy flashcards.
